title: Improving teaching: getting over the knowing-doing hump -knowing-doing-hump/
author: Paul Cline
summary: Paul Cline uses his own two-year failure to set up a visualiser -- a tool he actively champions in CPD sessions -- to explore why teachers who know a practice would help still don't act on it. He cites Peps Mccrea's framing of three distinct causes of the "knowing-doing gap": not knowing how to enact an idea (fixed by modelling), knowing how but lacking fluency (fixed by rehearsal and coaching), and knowing how but failing to break old habits (fixed by cues and if-then habit prompts). Drawing on Mary Kennedy's "persistent problems of teaching," Cline argues there's a frequently neglected fifth problem -- accommodating personal needs -- and reframes the knowing-doing gap as a "hump" rather than a chasm: he already knows why and how to use a visualiser, he just hasn't been nudged over the threshold where the investment feels worth it right now. He connects this to a broader argument about experience: a novice teacher might get transformative value from a new tool, while an experienced teacher may only see marginal gains from the same tool, because they've already built workarounds to the problems it solves. Cline closes by arguing that coaching's real power may be providing external, concrete evidence of blind spots teachers can't see in their own practice, which can nudge a stalled problem back up the priority list even without solving it outright.
points: Cline applies Peps Mccrea's three-cause model of the knowing-doing gap (don't know how, know how but lack fluency, know how but haven't broken the habit) to his own unused visualiser as a live case study.

He reframes the gap as a \"hump\" rather than a chasm for experienced teachers who already know why and how to do something -- what's missing isn't knowledge but sufficient motivation to prioritise it over competing demands.

Cline extends Mary Kennedy's four persistent problems of teaching with a fifth, under-discussed one -- accommodating personal needs -- arguing PD often fails because it doesn't fit teachers' own priorities and working styles.

He argues a tool's value is relative to experience: a novice teacher may get a \"quantum leap\" from adopting something like a visualiser, while an experienced teacher may see only marginal gains because they've built other solutions to the same problem.
quotes: I never use one. I do have one, but haven’t touched it for about 2 years.
This isn’t a post about visualisers though. It’s about why getting teachers to change anything about their practice is really hard.
Peps Mccrae summarises this nicely in this thread, and suggests one of three problems that lead to this gap, and some potential solutions
Perhaps it might be better to think of the distance between knowing and doing as a hump rather than a gap.

For a novice teacher, perhaps a visualiser would represent something of a quantum leap, allowing them to do a whole host of things they weren't doing before. But for more experienced teachers it may be that there is only a marginal gain to be had.
The insight provided by a coach may result in sufficient motivation to nudge us over that hump.
